title: Why Exit Velocity and Launch Angle Don’t Tell the Whole Story
text: Two baseballs do not have to have the same exit velocity and launch angle to both be home runs. Exit velocity measures how fast the ball leaves the bat, while launch angle measures the vertical angle at which the ball is hit. These two factors work together, but there is not one specific combination that guarantees a home run. For example, one ball might leave the bat at 105 mph with a 25-degree launch angle, while another might leave at 95 mph with a 30-degree launch angle. Depending on other factors, such as where the ball is hit and the conditions of the stadium, both could still result in home runs.

title: Why Exit Velocity and Launch Angle Don’t Tell the Whole Story

Distance Variation in the “Sweet Spot”
Even when two balls are hit squarely into the ideal home run zone—between 100–105 mph exit velocity and 25°–30° launch angle—environmental conditions, ballpark dimensions, and spray direction cause actual travel distances to vary dramatically:

title: Why Exit Velocity and Launch Angle Don’t Tell the Whole Story
section: The Hidden Factors Behind Every Home Run
text:
The Hidden Factors Behind Every Home Run
Why do balls struck with identical exit speed and angle land anywhere from 330 to 450+ feet? Three major factors explain the gap:






Tip1. Asymmetrical Ballparks



Unlike football fields or basketball courts, no two MLB outfields are identical. A 315-foot fly ball down the line can be a home run in Boston or New York, but a 410-foot drive to dead center in Detroit or Colorado is often an easy out.








Tip2. Atmosphere & Weather



Air density directly influences aerodynamic drag. Warm air, low humidity, and high altitude (like Denver’s Coors Field, 5,200 feet above sea level) allow batted balls to carry several feet further than in cold, heavy sea-level air.

title: Park Effect: Which Ballparks Helped the Most?
text:
The same swing does not travel the same way in every ballpark. A home run in one stadium can be a warning-track out in another, even when the exit velocity and launch angle look nearly identical.
This page uses Statcast home-run data to compare how much a ballpark seems to boost or suppress home-run carry. Instead of treating every home run as identical, we compare each stadium’s median home-run distance to the season-wide median and ask: which parks were most generous to hitters in 2025?

What this plot is showing

title: About Me
text:
About This Project

This project explores the physics and mechanics behind Major League Baseball home runs using Statcast tracking data from the 2025 season.

title: About Me
section: What Makes a Home Run Go Out of the Park?
text:
What Makes a Home Run Go Out of the Park?
Sending a baseball over an outfield wall 350 to 420+ feet away requires the right combination of physics and timing:

Exit Velocity (Bat Speed & Contact): The ball needs sufficient speed coming off the bat. Most home runs require an exit velocity of at least 95–100+ mph to overcome aerodynamic drag and carry the fence.
Launch Angle (Lift): Crushing the ball is not enough if it is driven into the ground or popped straight up. The ideal trajectory is between 25° and 35°, which provides the perfect blend of carry and distance.
The Sweet Spot (“Barrels”): Statcast defines a “barrel” as a batted ball hit with the combination of exit velocity and launch angle that yields the highest likelihood of extra-base hits and home runs.

By studying these tracking metrics, we can see exactly what separates a routine flyout from a tape-measure blast.






TipData Source & Methodology




Data Source: MLB Statcast tracking data via Baseball Savant.
Scope: All regular and postseason home runs recorded during the 2025 MLB season.
Tools: Built using R, Quarto, the tidyverse, and plotly.

title: Why the Park Matters
text: A ball hit hard and high is not always a home run. The same launch profile can mean a no-doubter in one stadium and a routine fly ball in another. The shape of the park changes what a good swing actually looks like.

title: Why the Park Matters
text:
The hidden variable: the fence
Most discussions of home runs focus on exit velocity and launch angle. Those are important, but they do not tell the whole story. A 104 mph ball with a 28-degree launch angle may be a home run in one ballpark and a deep warning-track out in another.
That difference comes from the geometry of the stadium itself.

Some parks have short distances down the foul lines.
Some have deep center fields.
Some create stronger carry because of altitude, air density, or outfield angle.
Some are symmetrical; others are not.

The result is that the same swing can mean different things depending on where the batter stands.

title: Why the Park Matters
text:
A real-world possibility
Consider two very similar balls.
One is a 103 mph line drive with a 30-degree launch angle. The other is a 101 mph fly ball with a 29-degree launch angle. Both are strong, quality contact events. Yet one might land in the seats at Yankee Stadium or Fenway Park, while the other could be a catchable out in a deeper park. The difference is not just power. It is also the angle of the hit, the direction of the spray, and how far the fence sits in that direction.
This is why a home run should not be judged only by the launch data. It is also a product of the stadium architecture.

title: Why the Park Matters
section: Why park shape matters so much
text:
Why park shape matters so much
The fence is not a perfect circle. It bends and curves in different directions, and the distance from home plate changes all over the field.
A right-handed hitter whose ball is pulled to the left field line may be rewarded by shorter fence distance in one stadium but punished by a large dead-ball area in another. A ball hit to straightaway center may clear the fence in a park with 410-foot center field but die at the warning track in a park with 390-foot center field.
This means that the same launch profile can produce different outcomes simply because the path of the ball intersects a different part of the fence.

title: Why the Park Matters
text:
The bigger idea: park-adjusted baseball
This is why park effect is such a useful concept in baseball analysis. A ballpark is not a neutral backdrop. It changes the interpretation of a hit.
When we compare raw home-run distances, we are comparing outcomes that may have been shaped by different environments. If a hitter produces a certain type of contact in a hitter-friendly park, the raw data may exaggerate how strong that contact really was. In a tougher park, the same contact may look less impressive even if the swing itself was excellent.
That is why ballpark-adjusted analysis is so important:

It gives a clearer picture of true power.
It helps compare hitters across teams and parks.
It shows that a home run is not just a function of the swing but also of the stadium that surrounds it.

title: Why the Park Matters
text:
The takeaway
Every home run is a combination of three things:

The hitter’s contact quality.
The ball’s flight path.
The stadium it is flying in.

The best baseball analysis does not act like these are separate stories. It recognizes that the stadium is part of the outcome.
That is the key lesson from this project: a great swing is real, but the park can make that swing look even better or much worse than it otherwise would be.






TipFinal idea



A home run is not just a number on a Statcast sheet. It is a physical event shaped by the batter, the pitch, the ball, and the park itself.

title: Simulator
Elements of a Home Run
text:
What does it take to hit a home run in Major League Baseball? Using Statcast tracking data from the 2025 season, this interactive visualization examines how exit velocity and launch angle combine to send the ball over the fence.

Hitting a home run requires a precise combination of swing mechanics and launch characteristics. Mechanically, a hitter generates explosive rotational power from the lower body through the hips and torso, delivering high bat speed along a slightly upward swing plane to make square contact on the lower half of the baseball. This collision creates the signature characteristics of a home run: an exit velocity typically topping 100 mph, a launch angle elevated into the 25°–35° window, and backspin that generates aerodynamic lift to carry the ball beyond outfield fences 380+ feet away.












NoteKey Insights from the Data




Exit Velocity (x-axis): The speed at which the ball leaves the bat in miles per hour. Most home runs require at least 95 mph, with the median hovering around 105 mph.
Launch Angle (y-axis): The vertical angle of the hit in degrees. The optimal trajectory for a home run falls between 25° and 35°.
Hit Distance (Color): Lighter yellow and orange tones represent tape-measure blasts (400+ ft), while darker purple points mark shorter hits that just cleared the fence.
The “Sweet Spot”: Notice how the density of dots clusters heavily between 100–110 mph and 25°–35°. This combination produces the highest likelihood of a home run in Major League Baseball.
